paper.title: Patterns of service contacts for children who have experienced maltreatment and are known to social services: a Linked Routine Administrative Data Study in Wales, England and Denmark
paper.journal: International Journal of Population Data Science
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed. The abstract states only that the study is part of the European Commission Horizon Health 2024 SERENA project; no DST project reference is given.

registers.name_in_paper: routine administrative data on health (hospital admissions, emergency care, general practice)

linkages: Children recorded in child protection (CP) and children looked after (CLA) registers in Wales, England and Denmark are linked to their routine administrative data on health, education, employment and justice.
Children known to social services are matched to a propensity-matched cohort of children not known to social services.

sample.universe: Children recorded in child protection (CP) and children looked after (CLA) registers in Wales, England (Growing up in England and ECHILD) and in Denmark, plus a propensity-matched cohort of children not known to social services. The preliminary findings reported are from Wales only.
sample.unit_of_observation: child (individual), followed across the observation window
selection_rules: children recorded in child protection (CP) registers
children recorded in children looked after (CLA) registers
comparison cohort: a propensity-matched cohort of children not known to social services
observation window: from two years before to two-ten years after social service involvement

construction_notes: The abstract prints no sample size, no study period and no table or figure.

No Danish register is named individually: the abstract says only 'in Denmark with their routine administrative data on health (hospital admissions, emergency care, general practice), education, employment and justice', so no DST code can be assigned.
The comparison cohort is formed by propensity matching; the matching variables are not named.
The observation window runs from two years before to two-ten years after social service involvement.
Results are to be presented by each country; the only results stated in this abstract are preliminary findings from Wales.

claims.statement: Children in Wales recorded on the child protection (CP) register use emergency departments more than a propensity-matched cohort of children not known to social services.

treatment.label: being recorded on the child protection (CP) register

key_assumptions.assumption: The exposed sample is conditioned on maltreatment having been identified by and recorded with social services; maltreated children never identified by social services are not in the exposed group.

Common support: for children known to social services there exist children not known to social services with comparable propensity scores to match them to.

ambiguities: The paper is a one-page conference abstract: it prints no table, no figure and no numbers, so every magnitude field is null with an absent record rather than a transcription.
The reported findings are explicitly preliminary and from Wales only; the Danish (and English) analyses are described as planned, not reported.
The abstract reports no statistical test, so statistically_significant is left null rather than inferred from the wording.
The abstract calls the comparison group 'the matched general population'; it is taken to be the propensity-matched cohort not known to social services described in the methods.
Polarity of emergency department use is set relative to the concept of health-service utilisation (higher = more use); read as a health measure it would point the other way.

evidence.how: Looked at the whole one-page abstract: it contains no table, no figure and no numbers at all -- no point estimate, standard error, confidence interval or p-value is printed for this comparison.
The abstract names no estimator, regression model, control variables, clustering or weighting scheme; it says only that the comparison cohort is propensity-matched.
No sample size, cohort count or study period is printed anywhere in the abstract.
No control-group mean, pre-period mean or outcome standard deviation is printed; there is no summary-statistics table.
The abstract reports no statistical test, significance level or stars for the preliminary Wales findings, which it states in words only.
